about: The rubrics call the sentence before Pater noster the preface of the Lord's Prayer. After et ne nos indúcas in tentatiónem, they assign the response sed líbera nos a malo to the server. At low Mass the faithful may say the whole Our Father with the priest, in Latin, and add the Amen with him.

seg.tr: Taught by precepts that lead to salvation and formed through divine instruction, we dare to say:

fn.w004: A participle agreeing with the unexpressed nos, the subject of audémus.
fn.w007: Ablative of means with formáti. Here institutio means instruction: formed by divine teaching.
fn.w008: A participle agreeing with the unexpressed nos, the subject of audémus.
fn.w009: “Audémus dícere” expresses filial boldness: instructed by Christ, we dare to say “Our Father.”

seg.nr: The priest spreads his hands, and keeps them so through the prayer.

seg.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven,

fn.w011: Vocative singular in direct address to God.
fn.w012: Vocative masculine singular agreeing with Pater.
fn.w014: After the vocative the relative clause keeps the 2nd person: “who art”, not “who is”.
fn.w016: Ablative plural after in. The received English renders it in the singular.

fn.w017: Third-person present passive subjunctive expressing a petition.
fn.w019: Nominative neuter singular agreeing with nomen.

fn.w020: Third-person present active subjunctive expressing a petition.
fn.w022: Nominative neuter singular agreeing with regnum.

seg.tr: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

fn.w023: Third-person present subjunctive of fio expressing a petition.
fn.w025: Nominative feminine singular agreeing with volúntas.

seg.tr: Give us this day our daily bread.

fn.w033: Accusative masculine singular agreeing with panem.
fn.w034: Accusative masculine singular agreeing with panem.

seg.tr: And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

fn.w040: Dative of the person forgiven with dimítte.
fn.w041: Accusative plural. Literally debts. The received English has trespasses.
fn.w042: Accusative neuter plural agreeing with débita.
fn.w043: Introduces the comparison with our forgiving.
fn.w044: Et has the adverbial sense also here.
fn.w046: Present indicative, in contrast to the petitionary subjunctives.
fn.w047: Dative plural indirect object of dimíttimus. Literally debtors.
fn.w048: Dative masculine plural agreeing with debitóribus.

seg.tr: And lead us not into temptation,

fn.w050: Negates the independent subjunctive indúcas to form a prohibition.
fn.w052: Second-person present subjunctive in a prohibition with ne.
fn.w053: Governs the accusative to express direction into.

fn.w056: The embolism that follows begins with the same imperative: Líbera nos, quǽsumus, Dómine.
fn.w059: This edition parses “malo” as the neuter noun for evil. The following embolism takes it up in the neuter plural, “ab ómnibus malis.” The Catechism also explains that the petition ultimately refers to the Evil One (CCC 2851).

nt.w059: The form is the ablative of both words at once. It can be malum, evil as a thing, or malus, the Evil One. Neither the form nor the sentence decides, and the tradition reads it both ways. This edition takes malum and marks the doubt.

fn.w060: This Amen is said by the priest.
